newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dismisses Burma drug link claim.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dismisses Burma drug link claim.

text.p: Singapore has filed a protest with Australia's Special Broadcasting Service (SBS) over allegations of a link between investments by the city-state and a Burmese drug lord, Singapore media reported on Friday.

The Singapore High Commission in Canberra wrote to SBS on October 26 about a "Dateline" television programme earlier in the month that made the claims regarding the Singapore Government Investment Corporation (GIC).
"Dateline's innuendos are preposterous," said the letter from High Commissioner Winston Choo, which was made available to Reuters on Friday.

"Our laws against drug trafficking are among the world's toughest," Choo said in his letter to SBS managing director Malcolm Long. "It is therefore absurd to suggest that the GIC would undermine our efforts to keep Singapore drug free by knowingly supporting or condoning activities connected with the illicit drug trade."

Choo said the GIC's investment in the Myanmar Fund, one of the issues raised in the programme, "is transparent and it has publicly disclosed that it has an investment of 21.5 percent worth US$10 million in the fund".
The executive producer of the programme, Adrian Herring, told Reuters in Australia on Friday: "We stand by our story 100 percent."

A statement from SBS said it was going to present another programme with excerpts from the original and developments since it was aired. The statement said the Singapore High Commissioner had been invited to appear on the programme to discuss the issues but had declined.

Singapore opposition politicians Chee Soon-Juan and Jafar Ahmad said in a statement on Thursday that the programme had alleged that GIC funds were invested in projects linked to a Burmese drug lord. They did not elaborate.

Singapore has tough anti-drug laws, including a mandatory death sentence for anyone over 18 years found guilty of traficking in more than 15 grams (half an ounce) of heroin, 30 grams (an ounce) of morphine or 500 grams (18 oz) of cannabis.

One Singaporean was hanged on Friday for drug trafficking, the prisons department said. More than half of the 280 people hanged for various offences in the city-state since the mid-1970s were found guilty of drug charges.
